variables.meaning: the coefficient matrix of the equation Ax = b to which Gaussian elimination is applied: reduced by elementary matrices, E₃E₂E₁A = U, and factored as A = LU or PA = LU; Preview Activity 5.1.1's 3 × 4 matrix, Activity 5.1.3's [1 2 1; −2 −3 −2; 3 7 4], Example 5.1.1's [2 −3 1; −4 5 0; 2 −2 2]
the matrix obtained from A by the first row operation of Gaussian elimination, A₁ = E₁A
the matrix obtained after the second row operation, A₂ = E₂A₁ (Exercise 5.1.7)
the matrix obtained after three row operations of Gaussian elimination, A₃ = E₃E₂E₁A, with zeros below its first two pivots
the matrix A′ obtained from A by two row replacement operations in Activity 5.1.3, E₂E₁A = A′, one replacement short of the upper triangular U

the elementary matrix that performs the first row operation of Gaussian elimination by left multiplication, E₁A = A₁; for a row replacement it is lower triangular, and its inverse E₁⁻¹ performs the opposite replacement
the elementary matrix that performs the second row operation of Gaussian elimination, so that E₂E₁A is the matrix after two steps
the elementary matrix that performs the third row operation of Gaussian elimination, so that E₃E₂E₁A = U is upper triangular

the lower triangular factor of A = LU, L = (E₃E₂E₁)⁻¹ = E₁⁻¹E₂⁻¹E₃⁻¹, lower triangular because the elementary matrices of row replacements are, with 1s on its diagonal; the equation Lc = b is solved by forward substitution

the upper triangular matrix Gaussian elimination arrives at, U = E₃E₂E₁A, the upper triangular factor of A = LU or PA = LU; its diagonal entries are the pivots, and Ux = c is solved by back substitution

the permutation matrix that records the row interchanges of Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting, which linear algebra software provides so that PA = LU; to solve Ax = b one multiplies b by P and solves Lc = Pb, Ux = c
the unknown vector of the equation Ax = b, found from the factorization A = LU by solving Ux = c after c has been found
the right-hand side of the equation Ax = b; once A = LU is known, a new b costs only the two triangular solves Lc = b and Ux = c
the first of two right-hand sides b₁, b₂ for which the equations Ax = b₁ and Ax = b₂ are to be solved with the same matrix A, whose Gaussian elimination steps are nearly identical
the second of two right-hand sides b₁, b₂ for which Ax = b₁ and Ax = b₂ are to be solved with the same matrix A
the unknown vector c = Ux introduced to trade the equation Ax = L(Ux) = b for the two triangular equations Lc = b and Ux = c; c = [8, 3, 3] in Example 5.1.1
the components c₁, c₂, c₃ of the vector c, read off one at a time from the lower triangular equation Lc = b by forward substitution
the first unknown of a linear equation in two or three unknowns, the first coordinate of a point (x, y) or (x, y, z)
the second unknown of a linear equation in two or three unknowns, the second coordinate of a point (x, y) or (x, y, z)
the number of rows and of columns of a square matrix, the measure of its size in counting the effort of row reduction
the 3 × 3 matrix B = [3 −1 2; 2 −1 1; 2 1 3] of Activity 5.1.4 f, whose factorization PB = LU has a zero on the diagonal of U, so that B is not invertible
the 3 × 4 matrix C of Activity 5.1.4 g, whose null space is that of the U in its factorization PC = LU, since P and L are invertible
the identity matrix, whose product with any vector x is Ix = x
the inverse of A, rarely computed in practice and best found from the factorization PA = LU as A⁻¹ = U⁻¹L⁻¹P, since P is its own inverse (Exercise 5.1.6)
the inverse of the lower triangular factor L, relatively efficient to find because L is triangular (Exercise 5.1.6)
the inverse of the upper triangular factor U, relatively efficient to find because U is triangular (Exercise 5.1.6)
the determinant of A, which the factorization gives as det A = det L det U = det U, plus or minus the product of the pivots on the diagonal of U when PA = LU (Exercise 5.1.8)
the null space of a matrix; Nul(C) = Nul(U) when PC = LU, since P and L are invertible, so a basis of Nul(C) is read from the triangular U
the column space of a matrix; Col(A) need not equal Col(L) when A = LU, since L is invertible while A may not be (Exercise 5.1.10)

a square matrix whose eigenvalues and eigenvectors are approximated numerically by the power method: the positive stochastic matrix [0.7 0.6; 0.3 0.4] of Example 5.2.1, [2 1; 1 2] of Example 5.2.2, [0.5 0.2; 0.4 0.7] and [−5.1 5.7; −3.8 4.4] of Activity 5.2.2, the 4 × 4 matrix of Activity 5.2.4
the inverse of A, whose eigenvectors are those of A with the reciprocal eigenvalues λ⁻¹; the inverse power method applies the power method to A⁻¹ without computing it, solving Ax_{k+1} = x_k instead
the kth power of A, which carries the initial vector to the kth vector of the power method, x_k = Aᵏx₀ = c₁λ₁ᵏv₁ + c₂λ₂ᵏv₂
the identity matrix, whose product with any vector x is Ix = x
an eigenvalue of A, approximated numerically rather than found as a root of the characteristic polynomial; the multipliers m_k approach the eigenvalue λ having the largest absolute value

the dominant eigenvalue of A, the eigenvalue having the largest absolute value, which the power method finds: 1 for Example 5.2.1, 3 for Example 5.2.2, 0.9 and −1.3 in Activity 5.2.2, 16.35 for the 4 × 4 matrix of Activity 5.2.4

the eigenvalue of A having the smallest absolute value, found by the inverse power method as the reciprocal of the dominant eigenvalue of A⁻¹: 0.1 and 1 in the examples, 0.6 for [−5.1 5.7; −3.8 4.4], 0.75 for the 4 × 4 matrix
the third eigenvalue of the 4 × 4 matrix of Activity 5.2.4, −4.823, found by the inverse power method applied to A − sI for an s in the shaded ranges of Figure 5.2.3
the fourth eigenvalue of the 4 × 4 matrix of Activity 5.2.4, 7.526, found by probing another s between −λ₁ and λ₁
an eigenvector of A found by the power method, such as v = [3, 2] for [−5.1 5.7; −3.8 4.4]; it is also an eigenvector of A⁻¹ and of A − sI, with eigenvalues λ⁻¹ and λ − s
the eigenvector v scaled by the reciprocal of its component of largest absolute value, v̄ = [1, 2/3], so that Av̄ = [−1.30, −0.86] shows the eigenvalue −1.3 as the multiplier
the eigenvector associated to the dominant eigenvalue λ₁, which the normalized vectors x̄_k approach: [2, 1] in Example 5.2.1, [1, 1] in Example 5.2.2
the eigenvector associated to the second eigenvalue λ₂, whose contribution to x_k shrinks relative to v₁'s at every step: [−1, 1] in both examples; an initial vector x₀ = v₂ never detects v₁

a second eigenvector found by the power method from a different initial vector with the same eigenvalue, which shows that the dominant eigenvalue's eigenspace has dimension greater than one (Exercise 5.2.7)

the initial vector of the power method, x₀ = [1, 0] in the examples, written as a combination of eigenvectors x₀ = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂; for most choices it has some contribution from v₁, and an unfortunate choice such as x₀ = v₂ does not
the kth vector of the power method, x_{k+1} = Ax_k, so that x_k = Aᵏx₀; its direction approaches the eigenspace of the dominant eigenvalue while its length grows, until it is normalized
the first vector of the power method, x₁ = Ax₀; [2, 1] in Example 5.2.2
the second vector of the power method, x₂ = A²x₀ before normalizing, or x₂ = Ax̄₁ = [5/2, 2] once the vectors are normalized at each step
the third vector of the power method, x₃ = A³x₀

the normalized vector x̄_k = x_k/m_k, obtained by dividing x_k by its component m_k of largest absolute value, so that its own largest component is 1; the vectors x̄_k approach an eigenvector associated to the dominant eigenvalue
the first normalized vector, x̄₁ = x₁/m₁ = [1, 1/2] in Example 5.2.2
the second normalized vector, x̄₂ = x₂/m₂ = [1, 4/5] in Example 5.2.2
the third normalized vector x̄₃, drawn in the figure beside x̄₁ and x̄₂ approaching v₁

the component of x_k having the largest absolute value, the multiplier by whose reciprocal x_k is scaled to x̄_k; the multipliers m_k approach the dominant eigenvalue λ₁, and 1/m_k approaches the eigenvalue of smallest absolute value in the inverse power method
the multiplier printed at each step by the Sage command power(A, x0, N), the component of largest absolute value; for v̄ = [1, 2/3] the multiplier m = −1.3 is the eigenvalue itself
the number of steps taken in the power method, the index of x_k, x̄_k and m_k and the exponent of Aᵏ and λᵏ
the number near which an eigenvalue is sought; the inverse power method applied to A − sI finds the eigenvalue of A closest to s, as 1/m_k + s
the number of steps the Sage commands power(A, x0, N), inverse_power(A, x0, N) and find_closest_eigenvalue(A, s, x0, N) run

the eigenspace of the dominant eigenvalue λ₁ = 1 of the stochastic matrix of Example 5.2.1, to which the vectors x_k of a Markov chain draw close; finding a basis vector of E₁ this way is essentially how PageRank works
the eigenspace of the eigenvalue 3 in Exercise 5.2.7, whose dimension exceeds one when the power method finds two different eigenvectors for λ = 3
the steady-state vector q = [2/3, 1/3] of the stochastic matrix [0.8 0.4; 0.2 0.6], to which the Markov chain x_{k+1} = Ax_k of Preview Activity 5.2.1 converges
the weights c₁, c₂ of the initial vector as a linear combination x₀ = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ of eigenvectors, so that x_k = c₁λ₁ᵏv₁ + c₂λ₂ᵏv₂
the null space Nul(A − λI), whose basis gives the eigenvectors of λ; finding it on a computer is plagued by numerical problems, since round off can create a nonexistent pivot
the determinant in the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI), whose roots are the eigenvalues; finding it for a large matrix requires considerable computation
